description: I aim to bring together a passionate, creative, and collaborative group of individuals who share a common interest in space exploration, science, and innovation. Every member will have an opportunity to contribute ideas, take initiative, and apply their strengths while working towards a shared goal. Together, we aspire to transform our curiosity about space into meaningful innovation and create a project that reflects our dedication, creativity, and commitment to making a difference.
summary:
ARES (Astronaut Route & Exploration System) is an interactive Mars exploration guide that brings mission history and terrain planning into one experience. Its global explorer highlights major landing sites, named features, rover traverses, and selected sample locations. At Jezero Crater, a local route planner compares candidate paths using terrain elevation and slope, while distance tools help users explore locations.

The project addresses the challenge by turning planetary data and past mission records into a map that is easier to explore and understand. It connects where missions landed and traveled with the terrain they encountered, helping users compare locations and plan hypothetical routes.

ARES matters because future exploration depends on understanding terrain and learning from previous missions. The current version is a research and planning prototype, not a live navigation or landing-safety system; its routes and risk colors are illustrative and should not be used for operational decisions.
details:
ARES (Astronaut Route & Exploration System) is an interactive guide to Mars exploration. It combines a global explorer of notable Martian features and historic mission sites with a detailed route-planning view of Jezero Crater. Users can explore rover paths and selected sample locations, inspect mission-site information, measure distances between points, and compare two candidate routes generated from terrain elevation and slope data.

The project makes Mars data more approachable by connecting maps with mission history and clear visual explanations. It is designed for students, space enthusiasts, and early mission-planning exploration. Its intended impact is to help people understand how terrain influences exploration and why learning from past missions matters for future journeys.

ARES was built as a web application using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It uses Leaflet for the local terrain map, terrain data derived from a USGS Jezero Crater elevation dataset, and an experimental ArcGIS-powered 3D Mars globe. Route comparisons use pathfinding across the local elevation grid, with slope contributing to the route cost. The interface also includes NASA mission imagery and data-based rover traverse visualizations.

The creative element is bringing planetary science, mission storytelling, and map-style route exploration together in one interface. The team considered usability, readability, data sources, visual distinctions between route and terrain conditions, and the limits of available data. ARES is a student-built prototype: its route colors and slope-based comparisons are illustrative, and it does not provide live astronaut positioning or certified navigation or safety assessments.
